claims.claim: The Hebrew year 5786 (2025-2026 Gregorian) is a regular year in the 19-year Metonic cycle, NOT a leap year, so it has only one Adar (no Adar I / Adar II).

Hebrew calendar 2026 (Gregorian) holiday dates, recomputed 2026-08-09 against pyluach AND the Hebcal REST API (i=on, Israel schedule): Tu B'Shvat (15 Shvat) = Feb 2; Ta'anit Esther (13 Adar) = Mar 2; Purim (14 Adar) = Mar 3; Shushan Purim (15 Adar) = Mar 4; Pesach (15-21 Nisan) = Apr 2-8; Yom HaShoah (27 Nisan) = Apr 14; Yom HaZikaron (4 Iyar) = Apr 21; Yom HaAtzmaut (5 Iyar) = Apr 22; Lag BaOmer (18 Iyar) = May 5; Shavuot (6 Sivan) = May 22; 17 Tammuz = Jul 2; Tisha B'Av (9 Av) = Jul 23; Rosh Hashana (1-2 Tishrei 5787) = Sep 12-13; Yom Kippur (10 Tishrei) = Sep 21; Sukkot (15-21 Tishrei) = Sep 26 - Oct 2; Simchat Torah (22 Tishrei in Israel) = Oct 3; Chanukah (25 Kislev - 2 Tevet 5787) = Dec 5-12, 2026; 10 Tevet = Dec 20, 2026.
claims.verification_note: CORRECTION: the previous entry listed 17 Tammuz = Jul 3 and Tisha B'Av = Jul 24. Both were off by one day. Hebcal returns Tzom Tammuz 2026-07-02 and Tish'a B'Av 2026-07-23, and pyluach independently gives HebrewDate(5786,4,17) -> 2026-07-02 (Thursday) and HebrewDate(5786,5,9) -> 2026-07-23 (Thursday). Neither fast is postponed in 2026 because neither falls on Shabbat. SKILL.md and SKILL_HE.md were corrected. All 17 other dates in this entry re-verified OK against both sources.

claims.claim: pyluach is an open-source Python library for Hebrew calendar / Jewish date conversion, used as the canonical reference implementation for date arithmetic in this skill.
hebcal.com is the canonical web-based Hebrew calendar reference and provides authoritative holiday tables, dual-date conversions, and a developer API at hebcal.com/home/developer-apis.
5 Iyar 5786 falls on a Wednesday (April 22, 2026), so neither Yom HaZikaron nor Yom HaAtzmaut is displaced in 2026.
claims.raw_snippet: As a result, Independence Day falls between 3 and 6 of Iyar, and can be on a Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday.

claims.claim: Displacement rules for Yom HaZikaron and Yom HaAtzmaut avoid Shabbat desecration: 5 Iyar can only fall on Monday, Wednesday, Friday or Saturday; on Friday or Saturday the celebrations move up to the preceding Thursday (decided 1951), and since 2004 a Monday is postponed to Tuesday (6 Iyar).
claims.raw_snippet: To avoid Sabbath desecration , it was decided in 1951 that if the 5th of Iyar falls on a Friday or Saturday, the celebrations would be moved up to the preceding Thursday (3 or 4 of Iyar). Additionally, since 2004, if the 5th of Iyar is on a Monday, the festival is postponed to Tuesday (6 of Iyar).
claims.verification_note: CORRECTION: the skill previously said 'if it falls on Sunday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, no displacement'. The source states 5 Iyar can fall only on Monday, Wednesday, Friday or Saturday, so Sunday and Tuesday are impossible. SKILL.md and SKILL_HE.md were corrected to name Wednesday as the only no-displacement case.

claims.claim: Hebrew gematria uses letter-number mapping (alef=1, bet=2, ..., yod=10, kaf=20, ..., kuf=100, ..., tav=400) with two important exceptions: 15 is written tet-vav (not yod-heh) and 16 is tet-zayin (not yod-vav), to avoid spelling Divine names.
claims.raw_snippet: By convention, the numbers 15 and 16 are represented as ט״ו ‎ (9 + 6) and ט״ז ‎ (9 + 7), respectively, in order to refrain from using the two-letter combinations י-ה ‎ (10 + 5) and י-ו ‎ (10 + 6), which are alternate written forms for the Name of God in everyday writing.

claims.claim: Pesach is celebrated for 7 days in Israel (15-21 Nisan) and 8 days in the diaspora (15-22 Nisan, with an additional last day yom tov sheni).
claims.raw_snippet: Begins 15 Nisan Ends 21 Nisan (22 Nisan in traditional Diaspora communities)
claims.verification_note: The same article states "Jews outside of Israel celebrate the festival for eight days."
